messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Patel, a 44-year-old chef, came to treatment years after fleeing violence as a refugee, still living as if catastrophe might break through the kitchen doors at any moment. He spoke only in fragments about what happened. He had escaped after an attack on a convoy of civilians moving toward the border, when a vehicle ahead of him was hit and the road filled with screaming, blood, and people thrown onto the ground. He remembered visible wounds with terrible clarity—the exposed flesh of a man he had tried to reach, the stunned faces, the sound of sirens arriving too late—and yet whenever he tried to tell the story fully, language failed him. He would stop, stare at the floor, and say he could not put the worst part into words. At other times he described it in a flat, detached way that frightened him almost as much, as if it had happened to somebody else; then, without warning, the numbness would break and he would be flooded with grief for those who died there while he lived.

Those broken, shifting memories had hardened into convictions about himself. When the images came back, what gripped Arjun was not only horror but the certainty that he had failed. He had come to believe he would never forgive himself for not doing more on that road, that surviving when others did not said something shameful about him, and that whatever kind of man he had once been had been permanently damaged there. He did not talk about these beliefs as ideas. To him they were settled facts, proven every time the memory returned in that wordless, numb-then-grieving form.

Over time, those convictions shaped how he moved through the world. Because he felt weak, guilty, and changed for the worse, he became excessively compliant whenever he sensed possible threat, trying to stay agreeable and invisible. At work, if a manager spoke sharply or a customer became demanding, he immediately softened his voice, apologized even when he had done nothing wrong, and rushed to please them. He also avoided anything that made him feel exposed. He disliked crossing open parking lots alone before dawn for his restaurant shift and would take longer routes along walls or wait for someone else to walk out with him. He kept away from police officers, security personnel, and anyone in uniform if he could, lowering his eyes and changing direction in the street. Each accommodation seemed sensible to him in the moment, but later it left him feeling humiliated and confirmed his belief that he was no longer the person he should have been.

His triggers were woven tightly into daily life. In the restaurant, ambulance sirens from the avenue outside could cut through the kitchen noise and instantly pull his attention away from the stove. If dishwashers or line cooks started talking about a car wreck they had passed on the highway, he felt his body tense before he had fully registered the words. Even seeing a delivery driver with a bandaged hand or a customer with a visible wound could make his chest tighten. He had begun to dread these moments, and because he dreaded them he was scanning for them constantly: listening for sirens, noticing injuries immediately, tracking snippets of conversation about accidents. The more on guard he stayed, the more often these reminders seemed to find him.

When he was triggered, Arjun did not simply feel upset; he became intensely watchful and had difficulty concentrating on whatever was in front of him. On the line he would lose track of an order while mentally locating exits from the kitchen and back door access through the alley, unable to settle until he knew exactly how he would get out. That constant planning for escape made unfamiliar places especially hard to tolerate, and even in familiar ones he remained superalert. In turn, this vigilant state seemed to sharpen the old memory rather than keep it away. A siren, an injury, or even his own sense that danger might be nearby could bring back the road in flashes he could not narrate, followed by either chilling numbness or a heavy wave of grief.

He tried to manage this by narrowing his world further. He avoided open spaces, avoided uniforms, steered away from conversations about accidents, and placated anyone who seemed potentially threatening. But these habits kept the fear alive. Because he left the room when accident stories began, the topic remained unbearable. Because he watched uniforms so carefully, they stood out immediately. Because he was always rehearsing escape, every setting felt as if escape might be needed. And because he kept yielding to others, he read his own behavior as proof of permanent damage and moral failure, which made him even more vigilant the next time.

What finally brought Arjun in was a recent evening service when an ambulance stopped outside the restaurant after a pedestrian injury nearby. A server came in describing the blood on the sidewalk, and Arjun froze at the pass, unable to focus on tickets, already mapping the exits and fighting the urge to disappear into the walk-in refrigerator. Later he sat in his car and cried with a grief he could barely explain. He said he was afraid that if this continued he would lose the only work that had given his life structure, and more than that, he was afraid he would remain forever the man who survived by doing too little. What he hoped for, quietly, was not to forget, but to be able to remember without feeling hunted by it.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state that Arjun’s negative beliefs or appraisals themselves lead to increased triggers or reminders.
The vignette does not explicitly convey that his sense of threat causes triggers or reminders to arise or become more salient.
The vignette does not clearly state that his maladaptive strategies directly lead to the trauma memory returning.
